name: Metric converter
seoDesc: Metric converter: work out temperature in degrees Fahrenheit from the length in inches and the area in hectares. A free conversion calculator with the…
summary: Give the Metric converter the length in inches, the area in hectares, the volume in US fluid ounces and the weight in grams and it returns temperature in degrees Fahrenheit. Think of it as a shortcut for a recipe, a shopping list, a travel plan or a form that asks for a unit you do not use. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Metric converter calculator work?
sections.html:
The Metric converter takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports temperature in degrees Fahrenheit in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the type of conversion); then you type in the length in inches, the area in hectares, the volume in US fluid ounces and the weight in grams.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 5 options, such as area, length and temperature. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in inches. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in hectares. The unit chip switches it to any of the 24 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in fluid ounces (US). The unit chip switches it to any of the 40 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in grams. The unit chip switches it to any of the 29 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Metric converter calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Temperature in degrees Fahrenheit=temperature in degrees Celsius
Temperature in degrees Celsius=temperature in Kelvins
Length in picometers=length in meters
Length in kilometers=length in meters
Length in centimeters=length in meters
Area in square centimeters=area in square millimeters

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Temperature, opening in kelvins
  • Temperature, opening in Fahrenheit
  • Temperature, opening in Rankine
  • Temperature, opening in Delisle
  • Temperature, opening in Rømer
  • Temperature, opening in Newton
  • Temperature, opening in Réaumur

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Metric converter earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Converting a figure someone quoted you so you can compare it
  • Filling in a form that asks for imperial or metric values
  • Reading a recipe written in units you do not use
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the length in inches, the area in hectares and the volume in US fluid ounces — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Metric converter calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns temperature in degrees Fahrenheit, derived from the length in inches, the area in hectares and the volume in US fluid ounces. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Metric converter calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the length in inches, the area in hectares, the volume in US fluid ounces and the weight in grams, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter temperature in degrees Celsius in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Temperature in degrees Celsius opens in Celsius and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Metric converter calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
